newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian patriarch vows to stay on despite ruling.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian patriarch vows to stay on despite ruling.

text.p: One of two rival patriarchs of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church said on Thursday he would not resign despite a decision by the Supreme Administrative Court declaring the registration of his synod null and void.

"It is not possible to withdraw as patriarch, not only because I do not have any grounds to but because I would commit a sin before God and would be betraying those who have elected me," Patriarch Maxim told reporters after talks with President Petar Stoyanov.

Maxim was appointed patriarch in 1971 by Bulgaria's former communist rulers. His opponents enthroned Patriarch Pimen in July last year, and it was Pimen who conducted the blessing ceremony when Stoyanov took office in January.
Maxim's opponents say he should be replaced because he was appointed rather than elected.
The court on Wednesday ruled the registration of Maxim's synod invalid for technical reasons, a decision which the synod's lawyer Nikolai Bankov dismissed as irrelevant.

"Pimen cannot be a patriarch as the church canon and rules, which are part of the religious law, have been breached. Apart from that, the Holy Synod has pronounced anathema (in 1996) on Metropolitan Pimen," he told Reuters.
He said that if Pimen's synod applied for registration, Maxim's synod would appeal. Both synods plan church councils later this year.

"Yesterday's decision of the Supreme Administrative Court is simply a cancellation of an administrative order and it cannot be taken as recognition or de-recognition of the leadership of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church," a statement from Maxim's synod said.
Pimen, who also met Stoyanov on Thursday, said Maxim should come to his synod's council so they could discuss their differences.

Maxim enjoys the support of the Bulgarian Socialist Party, while Pimen is closer to the Union of Democratic Forces, the main opposition in the parliament dissolved last month. Elections are due on April 19.

Stoyanov's blessing by Pimen was the first religious ceremony for a new head of state since Boris III became king in October 1918, and Maxim said the president had promised his help to reunify the church.
